reviews.text: My elderly dog ​​became lethargic, and they provided emergency care at night. They also readily agreed to let me take him to my regular vet the next day, which was a great help.

I lost my beloved dog during a neutering surgery.

I was surprised to see similar experiences in other people's reviews. The clinic said, "The bleeding won't stop, so please let us keep him overnight. We'll call you tomorrow," but I didn't hear anything from the clinic until I contacted them the next day.

When I called, they asked me to come pick him up. They briefly mentioned that his blood pressure the previous day (the morning of the surgery) was quite low, and apparently, under normal circumstances, the operation would have been stopped at that point.

After a night's rest, he still seemed unwell, so I took him to two other hospitals where he was admitted, and he passed away.

I regret my decision to choose this clinic at the time. However, the doctor is to blame.

I hope that no one or any dog ​​will ever have to go through the same experience.

My beloved dog died at this hospital.

The circumstances surrounding his death were unclear, so I waited for an answer, but they appointed a lawyer to represent him. I don't want to just accept it, so I'm currently preparing. This is unreasonable. Diary entry from May 22, 2021

Late night, October 12, 2020
My beloved miniature dachshund was breathing heavier than usual, so I contacted this nearby emergency hospital. The first thing the director said to me was, "After-hours treatment will cost an additional 18,000 yen. Is that okay?" I replied, "Yes, that's fine," and arrived at 2 a.m. with my dog's medical history and medications.

When my dog ​​showed signs of resistance during blood tests and X-rays, the director was a little rough with the Elizabethan collar. He buttoned it incorrectly and, with very clumsy hands, put it on at the tightest button. My husband said, "Doctor, that's too tight," so he loosened one button and refastened it.

The examination results showed that "He has pneumonia. It's not serious, but it will help him breathe easier, so it would be best to put him in an oxygen chamber." So he was admitted to the hospital.

I called the hospital that afternoon, and the receptionist said, "The director is examining him, so I'll call you back." I waited, but there was no call, so I called again at 4 p.m. and was told I would be there at 6 p.m.

The three of us went there together, and 12 hours later, we were able to meet our little one, and he was wagging his tail in joy, perhaps out of relief at seeing us. The director explained that he was eating and his heart rate was fine, but that taking him out of the oxygen chamber would cause him to become cyanotic, so it would be better to keep him in the hospital. He was also told that his life was not in danger and that he would recover in 3-4 days. There was no mention of any risk of a sudden change. His condition seemed better than I had expected, so for the first time, I was able to go home with peace of mind.

I was so worried the night before that I couldn't sleep at all, so I slept well that day.

However, just after 6 a.m. the next morning, we received news that he was in critical condition.
Shocked, I rushed to the hospital immediately and they were already performing CPR.
Not knowing what had happened or why, I kept talking to my child, but a few minutes later he took his last breath. It was so sudden and the shock was so great that I was filled with grief. More than wondering why it had happened, I felt a strong desire not to leave my child's side even for a moment.

However, as time passed, my questions grew: why had he died so suddenly? What had happened?

Six days later, I called the hospital to find out the reason, and the director's first question was, "What happened?" I was surprised by this. I normally expected to hear something like, "That's so unfortunate," or offer condolences.

I later found out that the Elizabeth curler had been worn even when the child was sleeping, and that the child had been placed in an oxygen chamber. I understand that it's fine to do this during tests, but I can't believe they would leave the Elizabeth curler on all the time when a child is having trouble breathing and just wants to sleep comfortably!! When I asked why, he replied, "I'm afraid I might get bitten," and "It would be a problem if the staff member who came in that morning got bitten," even though he wasn't bitten. I was truly shocked and speechless. Is the director not used to dealing with animals? I truly regret entrusting my precious life to such a person.

I cannot accept this and will continue to pursue this matter.

The dog passed away after two days in the hospital, but the fees were first-rate. Since we are paying first-rate fees, we should expect the examination, treatment, and management to be first-rate as well.

Aren't you ashamed of yourself as a doctor entrusted with lives!!?

I hope that no animal or owner ever has to go through this again.

I have been seeing him as my cat's family doctor for almost five years.
There is no waste in the tests, diagnoses, or treatments, and the entire process is very smooth.
He provides necessary explanations concisely and adopts a treatment plan that puts the animal first, making him an extremely trustworthy doctor.
I feel that he is not commercial, but rather takes essential veterinary care seriously.

I had a blood test done on the day of the surgery, and the results meant extra charges. The explanation was terrible; the blood test cost 20,000 yen, and the person on the phone was smoking while I was talking. You absolutely shouldn't go there.
I recommend going to Shinjuku Animal Hospital instead.

Thank you for your help during the night.

I really appreciate your kind and helpful service.

Also, I felt much more at ease after receiving a thorough explanation at my appointment the following week. ^_^
I look forward to your continued support.
